title: Little girl, get up (Mark 5:35–43)
hook: Mark keeps his Aramaic words, talitha koum, and then: give her something to eat

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hem of his garment: a woman reached for his clothes in the crowd, and he stopped to find her. Your line was daughter, go in peace. Who did you stop for? Day one hundred seventy-nine.

While Jesus is still speaking to the woman, men come from Jairus's house. And they say the sentence every parent dreads. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any more? Picture Jairus's face. He did everything right. He begged, he hurried, and the delay for someone else's healing cost him everything. Jesus overhears, turns to him, and says five words. Then he goes to the house anyway, where the mourners have already started wailing. What happens in that small room is one of the few places the Gospels keep Jesus's own words in his own language. Today's word: talitha koum.
screen: `YOUR DAUGHTER IS DEAD.` → `WHY TROUBLE HIM ANY MORE?` → `FIVE WORDS TO JAIRUS.`

segments.voice: The five words, in the old King James Bible: "Be not afraid, only believe." At the house, the crying is loud. Jesus says the child isn't dead but sleeping, and they laugh at him. So he sends everyone out except her mother and father and three disciples, Peter, James and John. Then, "he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Talitha koum. Mark wrote in Greek, but here he keeps the Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke at home, and then translates it for his readers. Talitha is a tender word, something like little girl. Koum means get up. It's what you might say to a child on a school morning. No grand formula. Just her hand in his and, little girl, get up. And she does. She gets up and walks around, and Mark adds, for she was twelve years old. The same twelve years the woman in the crowd had suffered. Then two closing lines, and both are so human. He tells them to keep it quiet. And he "commanded that something should be given her to eat." The miracle ends with a snack. Christians read this as a sign of Jesus's power over death, and of the hope of resurrection. But many love the ending most: after the impossible thing, the practical one. A child who's been very sick needs food. Care doesn't stop at the miracle. It goes on to the kitchen.
screen: `BE NOT AFRAID, ONLY BELIEVE.` · `HE TOOK HER BY THE HAND.` · `TALITHA KOUM: LITTLE GIRL, GET UP.` · `GIVE HER SOMETHING TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone today. Settle, and breathe. Let yourself hear it: talitha koum, little girl, get up. Said to a child, gently, holding her hand. Now think of someone who needs to get up from something: an illness, a grief, a long bad season. Then ask the practical question Jesus asked. What do they need to eat? Is there a meal you could bring, a coffee you could buy, a snack you could share? Choose one. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you plan it. The bell holds the time.
Talitha koum. Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke: little girl, get up. Mark kept the sound of it.
Your line: talitha koum. Today, help someone get up by doing the practical thing, and feed someone, even if it's only a snack. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians read this story at funerals and in times of serious illness as a sign of hope in the resurrection, and churches often answer illness and grief with meals brought to the family's door.

original.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters by Mark: little girl, get up. Some manuscripts read koumi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic phrase.
what it means: Aramaic for little girl, get up, said gently, holding her hand, and followed by something to eat.
what a scholar hears: one of the few places the Gospels keep Jesus's Aramaic. Mark translates it, and manuscripts vary between koum and koumi.

notes: The index word is 'talitha koum'; the KJV spells it 'Talitha cumi' (from the reading koumi). Both kept, and noted in the original and trapdoor.
'Talitha' as a tender word (some connect it with a word for lamb); stated only as 'something like little girl'. Confirm.
Original script given as the Greek transliteration (ταλιθα κουμ) rather than Aramaic script, to avoid guessing at pointing. Confirm or supply Aramaic.
Readings: power over death / resurrection hope, and practical care; confirm.
